subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins and serve as precursors for neurotransmitters, hormones, and energy. Their metabolism links the TCA cycle, nitrogen balance, and clinical states such as liver disease or inborn errors.

sections.p: Amino acids are obtained from diet or protein breakdown. They are deaminated, producing α‑ketoglutarate for the TCA cycle and ammonia for urea synthesis.
b: Transamination transfers amino groups between amino acids and α‑keto acids
Deamination removes the amino group, generating ammonia

sections.p: Transaminases (ALT, AST) use pyridoxal‑5′‑phosphate (vitamin B6) as a co‑factor. The resulting α‑keto acids enter the TCA cycle, while ammonia is detoxified in the liver via the urea cycle.
b: Pyridoxal‑5′‑phosphate is essential for all transamination reactions
Glutamate is the central amino‑group carrier
Urea cycle converts ammonia to urea for renal excretion

t.b: Is there hepatocellular injury? Elevated enzymes suggest liver damage affecting amino‑acid handling
Is ammonia accumulation present? High levels indicate urea cycle failure or severe liver disease
Is pyridoxine deficiency contributing? Low B6 impairs transamination, causing seizures in infants

sections.p: The liver controls nitrogen balance through the urea cycle, while hormonal signals (insulin, glucagon) modulate protein synthesis and breakdown.
b: Insulin promotes amino‑acid uptake and protein synthesis
Allosteric regulation of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I by N‑acetylglutamate

sections.p: Inborn errors (e.g., maple‑syrup urine disease), liver failure, and vitamin B6 deficiency disrupt amino‑acid metabolism, leading to toxic metabolite accumulation.
b: Maple‑syrup urine disease: branched‑chain α‑ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency
Hyperammonemia: urea cycle defects or acute liver failure
Pyridoxine deficiency: seizures, irritability in infants

t.b: Which amino acids are elevated? Pattern points to specific inborn errors
Are toxic metabolites present? Detects branched‑chain ketoacids in MSUD

sections.p: Abnormal amino‑acid metabolism presents as neurologic crises, hepatic encephalopathy, or growth failure. Recognising patterns guides urgent therapy.
b: MSUD crisis → feeding intolerance, lethargy, sweet odor
B6 deficiency → infantile seizures, peripheral neuropathy

sections.p: Focus on the link between transamination, the urea cycle, and clinical presentations of ammonia toxicity or vitamin B6 deficiency.
b: Elevated ALT/AST with low B6 suggests hepatic failure impairing transamination
High plasma leucine, isoleucine, valine = MSUD
Ammonia > 100 µmol/L in a child with vomiting = hyperammonemic crisis

whenToSeekHelp: New onset seizures in an infant (possible B6 deficiency or metabolic disorder)
Rapidly worsening lethargy and sweet‑smelling urine (suspect MSUD crisis)

faq.q: Why does liver disease cause high ammonia?
faq.a: Damaged hepatocytes cannot run the urea cycle, so ammonia accumulates and crosses the blood‑brain barrier.

faq.q: What is the role of vitamin B6 in amino‑acid metabolism?
faq.a: B6 (pyridoxal‑5′‑phosphate) is the co‑factor for all transaminases, enabling amino‑group transfer.

faq.q: How is maple‑syrup urine disease treated acutely?
faq.a: Stop protein intake, give high‑calorie glucose, and use dialysis to remove branched‑chain ketoacids.

exam: Explain how a defect in carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I leads to hyperammonemia and its clinical signs.
Describe the biochemical basis of seizures in pyridoxine deficiency.
Interpret a plasma amino‑acid profile showing elevated leucine, isoleucine, and valine.
